items.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

AI can provide multimodal content, personalised scaffolding, flexible participation and assessment, and support for self-regulated and collaborative learning. items.title: Weather warnings for a multilingual nation: The role of applied linguistics in the National Weather Service’s AI Language Translation Program

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

items.title: Explainable AI for tail-risk forecasting in cryptocurrencies: evidence from green and energy-intensive assets for risk-aware investment decisions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to develop an explainable deep learning framework for forecasting tail risk and volatility in cryptocurrency markets, with a particular focus on differences between energy-intensive and ESG-oriented digital assets. It aims to assess how volatility dynamics and downside risk exposure vary across environmental profiles and market regimes and how these differences can inform risk-aware investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach The proposed framework uses a quantile long short-term memory model to estimate predictive quantiles and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), enabling the modeling of asymmetric, fat-tailed and regime-dependent risks. The analysis focuses on four cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Litecoin (energy-intensive) and Algorand and Chia (lower-energy alternatives). The model integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations-based explainability and a regime classification (calm vs stress). Robustness is assessed using 20-, 40- and 60-day rolling evaluation windows, while predictive performance is evaluated through coverage rates, hit ratios and Kupiec and Christoffersen back testing procedures. Findings The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across the four cryptocurrencies rather than a uniform green-versus-energy-intensive ranking. Chia records the lowest Q50 root mean squared error (0.00149) and mean absolute error (MAE) (0.00119), whereas Algorand has the lowest full-sample CVaR (0.0293) and Litecoin the highest (0.0411). Regime results are also asymmetric: Bitcoin’s Q10 violation rate rises from 8.74% in calm periods to 11.74% in stress periods, while Litecoin and Algorand record more Q10 violations in calm than in stress regimes. Chia combines the lowest global Q10 violation frequency (2.98%) with the highest mean CVaR violation loss (0.127419), showing that infrequent breaches can still be severe. These findings support asset-specific tail-risk monitoring and cautious use of energy-profile information in risk-aware investment decisions. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating quantile-based deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, regime-specific diagnostics and sustainability considerations into a unified risk-forecasting framework. Its main value lies in complementing connectedness and spillover studies with interpretable, asset-level distributional forecasts and formal tail-risk backtesting. The results provide decision-support information for risk monitoring and portfolio analysis, but do not imply that lower-energy cryptocurrencies are universally safer or that the observed differences are causal.

items.title: The AI engagement paradox: algorithmic congruence and its inverted-U effect on tourist experience quality

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
items.abstract_text: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ). Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction. Findings AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward. Research limitations/implications This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy. Originality/value This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

items.venue: The International Journal of Information and Learning Technology
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transformed into research value within Southeast Asian universities by investigating the institutional and adaptive mechanisms linking technological capability to perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, the study develops the Institutionally Regulated Research Adaptability framework and tests it using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 2,371 respondents across 170 universities in eleven Southeast Asian countries, with institutional-level aggregation supported through within-group agreement and interclass correlation diagnostics. Findings The results demonstrate that institutional AI regulatory capacity exerts stronger effects on adaptive academic reconfiguration than foundational technological capability conditions. Dynamic research agility emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived research value realization. The proposed negative moderating effect of excessive regulatory readiness was not supported; instead, regulatory structures reinforced adaptive responsiveness. Importance–performance map analysis further identified dynamic research agility and regulatory-ethical framework readiness as the most critical strategic intervention priorities. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while institutional aggregation may mask within-university variation. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and comparative multi-group analyses to examine national-level institutional heterogeneity across higher education systems. Practical implications Universities should prioritize institutional AI governance maturity, strengthen adaptive research agility, and strategically align faculty capability development with regulatory frameworks to translate AI capability into sustainable research and commercialization outcomes. Social implications The study highlights how institutionally coordinated AI integration can strengthen regional research ecosystems, support responsible digital transformation, and enhance Southeast Asia's academic innovation capacity within emerging knowledge economies. Originality/value This study advances AI-in-higher-education scholarship by shifting analytical focus from technology adoption to institutionally coordinated value transformation. It introduces institutionally regulated research adaptability as a novel explanatory mechanism and provides one of the first large-scale multilevel empirical examinations of GenAI-enabled research transformation across Southeast Asian higher education systems.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to investigate the strategic futures of business-to-business (B2B) marketing by identifying the interlinked themes shaping its transformation, with particular attention to artificial intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting force embedded in sociotechnical and institutional developments. Design/methodology/approach A two-round Delphi study with 29C-level industry experts was conducted. Responses were coded into 192 thematic mentions across 16 themes, analyzed through co-occurrence mapping and classified in a dual-axis typology by perceived nature (opportunity vs challenge) and origin (sociotechnical vs institutional). Findings AI is central but rarely operates in isolation: it co-occurs with every other theme, functioning as the connective node between internal capabilities and external demands in interorganizational relationships. The typology reveals a statistically significant attribution asymmetry (χ2(1) = 40.23, p &lt; 0.001): internally buildable themes are framed as opportunities, externally imposed demands as challenges. items.abstract_text: Purpose This paper aims to reframe board gender diversity as a strategic governance capability rather than a symbolic initiative or universal performance lever. It explains inconsistent diversity–performance findings and clarifies when diversity may strengthen oversight in algorithmically mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on structured evidence mapping and interdisciplinary research in corporate governance, leadership, efficiency economics, organizational demography and artificial intelligence (AI) governance, the paper develops a structured integrative conceptual synthesis focused on power, expertise–authority alignment and technological oversight. Findings Diversity effects are contingent rather than automatic. Board gender diversity is most likely to strengthen governance when three enabling conditions are present: representation thresholds that convert presence into voice, expertise aligned with authority and inclusive power structures that enable challenge. Under algorithmic complexity, these conditions may strengthen oversight of bias, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, vendor dependence and technocratic capture. Practical implications Boards and policymakers should move beyond numerical representation to structural influence. Diverse directors should occupy consequential committees, have relevant expertise and decision rights and be supported by practices that enable challenge. Boards should evaluate participation, committee assignments and technology-governance structures so diversity contributes to accountability, risk oversight and resilience rather than symbolic compliance. Social implications Representation-focused reforms are insufficient when formal inclusion does not produce influence. More substantively inclusive governance can strengthen accountability and stakeholder responsiveness in algorithmic organizational environments. Originality/value The paper moves beyond the business-case debate by integrating intersectionality, governance, efficiency and AI-governance perspectives into a mechanism-based framework showing how board diversity becomes a strategic governance capability under algorithmic complexity.

items.title: Designing transparency in AI influencer marketing: a consumer–agency architecture

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a conceptual synthesis of influencer marketing, consumer psychology and human–algorithm interaction research. Findings This paper introduces the Consumer–Agency Architecture (CAA) framework, distinguishing between information, control and provenance transparency. CAA posits that effects of transparency on consumer outcomes are driven by reductions in reactance, whether affective or cognitive. Information transparency primarily mitigates affective reactance; control transparency reduces cognitive reactance; and provenance transparency can attenuate both. Lower reactance, in turn, can support the formation of affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. The framework further identifies boundary conditions that either strengthen or weaken the relationship between transparency and reactance. Research limitations/implications This paper proposes a conceptual framework that remains to be empirically tested. It also posits that transparency effects in AI influencer marketing are primarily driven by reactance, not gains in perceived authenticity. The developed model also assumes that transparency forms have distinct rather than additive or even nonlinear effects on cognitive and affective reactance. Such assumptions could be tested in future work. Practical implications Brands and platforms should treat transparency as a portfolio of design levers rather than a single disclosure: match the specific type of transparency to the focal objective, anticipate trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all transparency that can erode trust. Social implications CAA provides a consumer-welfare lens for governing AI-influencer ecosystems by clarifying how transparency can support consumer agency. Originality/value CAA frames transparency in AI-influencer marketing as a means of respecting and protecting consumer agency, offering a mechanism-based foundation for designing ethically grounded, trust-sustaining AI-mediated brand relationships.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses. Findings In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory. Research limitations/implications The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons. Practical implications Educators should require prompt logs, independent evidence checks, revision rationales and originality rubrics that reward local validation, assumption testing, judgment and distinctive venture logic. Social implications In emerging economies, AI can broaden access to entrepreneurial feedback and market knowledge, but inadequate guidance may yield generic ventures detached from local needs. Originality/value The study extends entrepreneurship education ecosystem thinking by treating AI as an active mediator of cognition and venture artifact production whose educational role depends on tool function, assessment design and institutional governance.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) digital humans, developed to mimic humans, have emerged as promoters in marketing. Although existing studies have identified that AI digital humans' anthropomorphism shapes marketing outcomes, the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism remains underexplored. Focusing on historical figure-inspired AI digital humans in tourism destination marketing, this study examines how their multiple anthropomorphic features influence consumers' responses under the Computers are Social Actors and Media are Social Actors paradigms. Design/methodology/approach An online survey (N = 435) was conducted in 2026. Respondents completed a questionnaire after watching a typical travel vlog featuring a historical figure-based AI digital human. Findings We revealed that voice, behavior and mental anthropomorphism influence consumers' parasocial interactions with AI digital humans, which subsequently affect consumers' attitudes toward tourism destinations. Mental anthropomorphism mediates appearance, voice and behavior anthropomorphism's effects on parasocial interactions. Furthermore, mental anthropomorphism's effect is conditioned by consumers' familiarity with the AI digital human's historical figure prototype. Research limitations/implications This study extends existing research by demonstrating that AI digital humans' multiple anthropomorphic features shape consumers' parasocial interactions, with historical figure familiarity serving as a moderator. However, nonprobability sampling and a single cultural context restrict generalizability, warranting cross-cultural research with probability sampling in the future. Practical implications This study provides practical insight into developing AI digital humans in tourism marketing. Marketers should systematically optimize their human-likeness across voice, behavioral and mental traits, while considering consumers' individual differences. Originality/value This study fills the research gap in AI digital humans by unpacking the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism and showing that its effects are contingent on consumers' traits.

items.abstract_text: Purpose While organizational knowledge conversion (OKC) is central to value creation, its translation into individual employee performance remains insufficiently understood, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled contexts where knowledge is abundant but must be appropriately adapted and ethically applied to generate meaningful outcomes. Against this backdrop, this study aims to empirically examine how OKC influences employee job performance (efficiency, effectiveness and quality) through customization knowledge utilization (CKU). Moreover, this study aims to investigate the moderating role of ethical AI climate (EAIC) among Gen Z employees working in AI-enabled hospitality workplaces. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave, time-lagged survey was conducted among 423 employees working in 3-, 4- and 5-star hotels in India. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS for measurement model, hierarchical regression and Hayes’ PROCESS macro to test mediation and moderated-mediation effects. Findings The results show that OKC significantly enhances employees’ job efficiency, effectiveness and quality. CKU partially mediates these relationships, indicating that knowledge should be adapted to task-specific contexts for greater performance outcomes. Furthermore, EAIC strengthens the indirect effects of OKC on performance via CKU, suggesting that ethical norms surrounding AI use enhance responsible and effective knowledge application. Originality/value This study extends the knowledge-based view and socialization, externalization, combination and internalization model by linking knowledge conversion to individual-level performance outcomes. By focusing on Gen Z employees, the study contributes to emerging knowledge management research on digital-native workforces in AI-enabled workplaces.

items.abstract_text: Connected health integrates sensors, mobile devices, and information technology to realize the real-time collection and transmission of medical data, providing patients with more personalized and efficient medical services. In this context, medical image segmentation technology plays a vital role as a key digital medicine tool in connected health. However, its effective deployment across diverse clinical settings and data sources remains challenging due to inherent variations in imaging modalities, patient demographics, and device characteristics. Currently, connected health requires highly efficient AI models for real-world medical applications. The versatility of the model across diverse environments is of great significance. Domain Generalization (DG) has emerged as a crucial solution to address these challenges of connected health. Previous work focuses on the domain similarity calculation on the final layer output of the backbone model, which ignores the impact of the multi-scale features. In this article, we proposed a Domain Pyramid Attention Network (DPANet), which aims to transfer knowledge from source domains to unseen domains for medical image segmentation at a multi-scale level. The overarching goal is to enhance the efficiency of connected health systems through this innovative knowledge transfer mechanism. DPANet is capable of learning multi-scale similarity between two kinds of domains through a Domain Similarity Pyramid Attention Module (DSPAM). We also designed Domain Prototypes (DP), which can enhance the flexibility of the knowledge pre-extracted from source domains for better transferability. A simple fusion method is adopted to merge the multi-scale features for the final segmentation prediction. DPANet is evaluated on Brain Tumor segmentation and Retina Fundus segmentation tasks, achieving an average Dice improvement of 1.14% and 0.98% on these two tasks, respectively.

items.abstract_text: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval. The findings not only confirm their adaptability in enhancing existing systems but also open up exciting possibilities for their deployment in specialised web information domains, paving the way for future research in this evolving field.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Deep learning (DL) frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch have powered major AI advancements, yet their reliance on third-party libraries introduces critical, understudied security risks. This article examines dependency management in these frameworks, focusing on dependency characteristics, associated vulnerabilities, and mitigation strategies. We analyze 448 libraries, 8,641 dependency-related commits, and 72 vulnerabilities, using GitHub APIs, official package sites, NVD/CWE databases, and a developer survey. Our findings show that while both frameworks share similar dependency types, PyTorch has more dependencies with less frequent updates. Both exhibit substantial vulnerabilities—42 in TensorFlow and 30 in PyTorch—almost half of which are high or critical severity, many unresolved. Notably, cumulative vulnerability exposure events reach 9,653 for TensorFlow and 627 for PyTorch, largely due to repeated removal and reintroduction of vulnerable dependencies. We also reveal that most security fixes occur incidentally alongside dependency optimization or compatibility improvements. Only 12% of changes explicitly address security, despite 90% of developers acknowledging its importance, reflecting limited experience, over-reliance on dependencies, and unclear accountability. This study sheds light on dependency management practices in DL frameworks, highlighting critical security risks and offering actionable guidance to strengthen DL ecosystem security and resilience.

AI-driven solutions therefore offer a promising direction for enabling adaptive and data-driven deployment decisions. items.abstract_text: Abstract Introduction: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often experience attention instability and emotion dysregulation. Existing interventions typically lack real-time responsiveness and ecological validity. This study retrospectively examined historical training records from an AI-assisted closed-loop system integrating emotion recognition and behavioral feedback for attention regulation in children with ADHD. Methods: This single-center retrospective analysis included historical training records from 60 children with ADHD who had completed either AI-assisted attention training or conventional attention training between 2021 and 2024. The AI-assisted training-record group comprised children whose archived records included 12 sessions of integrated cognitive training involving Go/No-Go, CPT, and Flanker tasks with real-time AI-generated feedback based on task performance and facial-emotion monitoring. The conventional training-record group completed the same attention tasks without AI-based feedback. Assessments included task performance, Conners Continuous Performance Test, 3rd Edition (CPT-3), teacher ratings, and emotion metrics, analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, linear growth modeling, and structural equation modeling (SEM). Results: Compared with conventional training records, AI-assisted training records showed greater pre-post changes in reaction time (RT), RT variability, and task accuracy, together with fewer commission errors in CPT-3. Post-feedback behavioral recovery was observed in 78.3% of feedback events. Teacher ratings showed consistent pre-post improvements across attention maintenance, emotional regulation, and task execution. Negative emotion labels decreased from 42.3% to 24.6% (p = 0.003). SEM supported an associative pathway linking emotion recognition frequency, feedback frequency, and RT reduction (95% CI: 0.15-0.38). Conclusions: The retrospective findings suggest that AI-assisted closed-loop training records were associated with favorable changes in attention and emotional-state indicators in children with ADHD. These exploratory results support further prospective, externally validated studies before broader clinical or educational implementation.

items.abstract_text: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

Originality/value The study treats generative AI not merely as a technological tool but as systems situated in different geopolitical contexts that can participate in shaping social-political discourse. items.abstract_text: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. items.abstract_text: Abstract Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Skin cancer incidence is rising globally, increasing pressure on dermatology services and making efficient triage increasingly important. AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial η ²=0.22; P <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; P <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation ( P =.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. The effect of advice source on adherence was fully mediated by trust. Conclusions Teledermatologist supervision of AI-based advice robustly increased patient trust and adherence intentions, particularly for high-risk assessments and concerned users. Our experiment is innovative in testing teledermatologist supervision in a population-level AI skin cancer app and in examining how motivational context shapes responses to advice. Unlike studies focused on postreferral teledermatology or chatbot-based advice, this study isolates the effect of hybrid AI-human advice in a store-and-forward screening context. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety.

The aim of the study is to provide a criteria-based evaluation of AI-assisted acoustic analysis as a methodological framework for research on legal prosody. items.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. items.abstract_text: Background Emergency medicine is characterized by urgency, criticality, severity, and diversity, which places high demands on undergraduate medical education. Although virtual simulation and case-based learning (CBL) have demonstrated benefits in medical education, their combined application in emergency medicine teaching has not been systematically evaluated, especially based on artificial intelligence (AI). Methods Third-year undergraduate students majoring in clinical medicine were selected as the research subjects and randomly divided into the control group and the experimental group. The control group adopted the traditional teaching method, while the experimental group adopted the AI-enabled virtual simulation combined with real emergency case teaching method. The learning situation of the virtual simulation platform was automatically recorded by the platform, and the teaching effect was evaluated through theoretical scores, objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) scores, clinical practice tracking evaluation (including advanced clinical ability and clinical transfer effect evaluation), comprehensive evaluation of learning psychology, and teaching satisfaction questionnaire. Results Compared with the control group, the students in the experimental group demonstrated significant advantages in all assessment dimensions, including theoretical test, various practical skills in OSCE, disease assessment, emergency management, clinical decision-making, as well as learning confidence, autonomous learning ability and teaching satisfaction ( P &lt; 0.001). The teaching effect can effectively transfer to the real clinical environment, and the diagnostic accuracy cultivated during the teaching process has important predictive value for the long-term clinical prognosis. This provides empirical evidence for the reform of emergency medicine education and emphasizes the importance of linking educational process evaluation with clinical outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.abstract_text: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
items.abstract_text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

items.title: Coping with sustainability information overload:  The role of generative artificial intelligence literacy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration
items.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations.

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: Having been studied for centuries, mathematical modelling is an important perspective in mathematics education; however, teachers often face difficulties in accessing appropriate and high-quality modelling activities for classroom use. This study investigates the capacity of ChatGPT and its customised version, the Mathematical Modelling Problem Generator (MMPG), to produce mathematically and pedagogically meaningful modelling problems. Four AI-generated model-eliciting activities were comparatively analysed: three produced in independent ChatGPT-4 sessions and one produced by MMPG, all focusing on ratios and proportions. The problem scenarios were evaluated using five characteristics from established frameworks, focusing on context (non-routine and real-life relevance) and complexity (multiple steps, uncertain solution paths, and multiple solutions). The results show that ChatGPT failed to produce MEAs that met key modelling characteristics, whereas MMPG successfully generated non-routine, multi-step MEAs with unclear solution paths and multiple valid solutions. Therefore, MMPG can be considered an effective tool for supporting pedagogical practice by improving teachers’ access to and design of content-aligned, high-quality modelling activities.

items.venue: Journal of Economics, Finance And Management Studies
items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and business analytics capability shape strategic financial decision quality in emerging market SMEs, with particular attention to the moderating role of AI governance maturity. Grounded in organizational information processing theory and dynamic capabilities theory, the study argues that better financial decisions depend not simply on access to advanced technologies, but on how effectively firms turn AI generated forecasts and analytical information into useful financial judgment. AI governance maturity is expected to strengthen this process by providing appropriate oversight, accountability, validation, and control over the use of AI generated financial information. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 385 respondents who possessed relevant knowledge of SME financial management, business analytics, AI applications, or organizational decision making. Data were collected using a five-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed with IBM SPSS version 26. Reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed, while Hayes’ Process Macro Model 1 was used to test the moderating effect. The results show that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability (β = 0.613) and business analytics capability (β = 0.487) both have significant positive effects on strategic financial decision quality. AI governance maturity also strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality, with an interaction coefficient of 0.518. These findings suggest that emerging market SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting tools are supported by sound analytical capabilities and governance practices. Effective financial decision making therefore requires not only better technology, but also the organizational capacity to interpret, review, and responsibly use AI generated financial insights.

items.abstract_text: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.

items.title: Emotionally Aware AI Chatbots for Adolescents: A Review of Psychological Principles for Learning, Calibrated Trust, and Healthy Human–AI Interaction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences
items.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

items.venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
items.abstract_text: The increasing use of automation and advanced machinery in modern industries has made equipment reliability and operational efficiency important factors in industrial production. Unexpected machine failures can interrupt production activities, increase maintenance expenses, and affect overall productivity. Traditional maintenance approaches, such as reactive and preventive maintenance, are often unable to identify early signs of equipment failure or accurately determine when maintenance is actually required. To overcome these limitations, this paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin technology for predictive maintenance in industrial environments. A Digital Twin is a virtual representation of a physical machine or industrial system that is continuously updated using data collected from sensors installed on the actual equipment. By combining this technology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms, it becomes possible to monitor equipment conditions, analyse operational patterns, detect abnormal behaviour, and predict potential failures before they cause major interruptions. The proposed approach integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, real-time data acquisition, data preprocessing, virtual equipment modelling, and AI-based predictive analysis into a unified maintenance framework. Machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be applied for fault detection, condition monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation. This paper presents a case-study-based investigation of AI-enabled Digital Twins for industrial equipment monitoring, with particular emphasis on understanding how real-time data and predictive analytics can improve maintenance planning. It also examines the system architecture, working methodology, potential advantages, implementation challenges, and limitations of the proposed approach. The study highlights the potential of integrating AI with Digital Twin technology to transform conventional maintenance practices into more intelligent, data-driven, and condition-based systems, thereby supporting improved equipment reliability, reduced unplanned downtime, and more efficient industrial operations. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twin, Predictive Maintenance, Machine Learning, Internet of Things (IoT), Industry 4.0, Fault Detection, Condition Monitoring, Remaining Useful Life (RUL).

items.title: Rethinking English Education In The Era Of Generative Ai And Global Englishes

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Arts, Humanities & Social Science
items.abstract_text: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.
